utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. Brashich, Mr. Kostich. My name is Mark Harmon, representing the Office of the Prosecutor. Appearing with me to my right, Mr. Tom Hannis and Ms. Magda Karagiannakis. To my left, the case manager, Ms. Carmela Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Dan Brashich and Nikola Kostich for the Krajisnik Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the Pre-Trial Conference in this matter. The position is this: Before we go any further, this Trial Chamber is engaged in another matter and therefore will not be in a position to try this case. It means that in due course, it will have to be assigned to another Trial Chamber. I refer to the trial of course of Mr. Krajisnik. We will invite the President to do that. Therefore, any orders we make at this conference are to some extent going to be subject to those of the Trial Chamber which will in due course try the case, and will be in many ways in a better position to judge matters than we are in a preliminary way. However, the rule bids us to set the number of witnesses the Prosecutor may call and also to determine the time available. It seemed to us on considering the matter that determining the time available may be a task which is realistically not one which we can perform, although we propose to make orders in relation to the number of witnesses, and that may assist in setting the time. There are, as we are aware, outstanding a number of issues in relation to admissibility. There is the whole question of the admissibility of evidence under Rule 92 bis, which has been before us. We will make orders in relation to that evidence, but they will be subject to review by the Trial Chamber. The position being this: That all the rulings as to admissibility, including those under Rule 92 bis, should be made in our view by the Trial Chamber actually trying the case. That Trial Chamber will be in a much better position to judge matters, having heard evidence and cross-examination, the trial having started, they will be in a better position than a Chamber which has heard no evidence and has merely got the various written pleadings to go on, to weigh the various matters related to admissibility and to accord them the necessary weight. It will also be the position that the Trial Chamber trying the case will have the issues clarified before it further than we have at the moment. So therefore all pending motions in relation to admissibility, they include the admissibility of, for instance, the intercepts, they should be dealt with by the Trial Chamber. We have in mind, in approaching this case, first of all to indicate a start date for the trial, if not precisely, in general terms, and also, as I said, to indicate, where necessary, the number of witnesses, and the approach which we have in mind in relation to the number of witnesses is to adopt the approach which we took in Milosevic, dealing with similar facts to these, where there were a large number of municipalities involved or a large number of incidents and it was a question of how best, given the time available, to approach the calling of evidence in relation to them. And we came to the conclusion in that case, we have in mind for this case, to indicate a broad number of witnesses who would be called per municipality, live, plus a number who could be called under Rule 92 bis, although, as I said in this case, that would have to be subject to the review or decision of the Trial Chamber as to whether those witnesses should be called live or not or called for cross-examination or not. It would then, if this -- we were to order this regime as we did in Milosevic, it would then be a matter of the Prosecution to make its selection of which witnesses it wished to call, live, which under Rule 92 bis. There being a large number of municipalities in this case, it's not possible at least at this stage to go into detail, at least at this conference. We'll hear submissions, but we have in mind making a more detailed scheduling order setting out how we propose that our orders should be given effect. But before we come to that, it may be sensible to hear whether there are any submissions or any matters which -- other matters which we should be dealing with. Perhaps I could turn to, having dealt with witness statements, untranslated documents, there are applications for admission of documents untranslated as of the 1st of July. Those again seem to be appropriate to be dealt with by the Trial Chamber which will be in a better position than we are to weigh up the various factors in relation to admissibility. The other matters which we have to deal with are exhibits. There do seem to be a very large number indeed, over 11.000, of which some 2.000 have been identified as core documents. We have in mind in relation to them to say that the core documents will be admitted, but given the huge number of other documents, they should only be admitted with leave but we will hear direct evidence about that one -- sorry, submissions about that. On relation to expert reports, we would wish to hear from the Defence about what their expert, Mr. Djunic has been doing. He's apparently been paid money for a written report, and there has been no sign of it. Now, we may be wrong about that, but we want to consider what he's been up to hear about that and decide what orders should be made. There is outstanding the matter of adjudicated facts. That's a matter which I believe is to be addressed by the 21st of November. We will -- obviously can't deal with that today but we can make an appropriate order in due course on that. Mr. Harmon? I should have mentioned the date. You'll be ready in mid-February, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. We will be ready by mid-February, assuming we get orders in due course prior to Christmas on the outstanding motions, because it will be then we will be in a position to make adjustments in the light but having considered that, having considered a variety of other elements, some of which I was unaware, that is the requirement that witnesses now in the Netherlands require a new passport, those elements, I think, are in the process of being discussed and being arranged and I think by mid-February we would be ready. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. As for the other -- while you're on your feet, the other matters I mentioned, I don't know if you want to address them or indeed any other matters you'd like to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course we will await the decisions of the Trial Chamber on the 92 bis applications, because it will be based on those decisions that we can make a reasonable plan, a trial plan, and a proper order of proof, so until we see the decisions in -- from the Chamber on that particular issue, which Your Honour has indicated would be in due course, we will make sufficient plans and deal appropriately with the decision and make all the necessary adjustments to meet a trial date in mid-February. In so far as other matters, I know Your Honour has been fully apprised by Ms. Featherstone of the matters that remain outstanding, and those matters were discussed at the Rule 65 ter conference. Your Honour has mentioned one, which is the expert reports, and Dr. Djunic's work and as Your Honour is aware, not only from Ms. Featherstone and the minutes of those meetings, but we have endeavoured for a considerable period of time to try to find a resolution on the issue of expert reports relating to exhumations. It is our position that that really is not an issue that needs to be litigated. It would be more properly discussed and resolved and we've attempted to find out what Dr. Djunic's specific objections are to the exhumation reports that have been submitted to him, and indeed, I understand he's in The Hague this week. I have even volunteered to meet with him personally to hear his objections. I would be prepared to meet with him at any time to address his concerns. As Your Honour is aware, in the course of trying to resolve the matter of the expert reports, the Defence raised a situation, an objection, saying that the -- their concern was that the exhumation reports were not linked to the specific events, the crimes, in -- identified in the schedules so in response thereto, my staff prepared what we called a linkage chart which was very precise. It linked the scheduled events to the witness statements and other disclosed material, and I have never been fully informed of what the objections are to that particular chart other than the allegation that it was superficial, but that is a chart that was presented to Ms. Featherstone as well for her examination. There was -- there is an outstanding issue on video clips that is a long-standing issue. The Defence, as Your Honour may recall, undertook to translate and prepare transcripts of video clips for which there were no transcripts. They complied in part with that, and they were to advise the Office of the Prosecutor sometime ago as to which of the video clips had not been properly or had not been transcribed. We have never received an answer to that effort. Other than that, Your Honour, I think that addresses the outstanding matters that are before the Trial Chamber. There is nothing further to add at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With regard to some of the issues that have been raised, and I'll take first the expert witness reports reviewed by Dr. Djunic. I have read the requirements of Rule 94 bis and the Defence has fully complied with that Rule and has put at issue the expert witness reports and we again demand cross-examination. Dr. Djunic was paid for his work in reviewing the expert witness reports in B/C/S. That was the brief that was given to him by me. He was not retained to make a written submission with regard to those expert witness reports but to give guidance to the Defence in interpreting the forensic witness reports. It is the position of the Krajisnik Defence that it is not for us, Pre-Trial, to educate the Prosecution with any defects that its expert witness reports may contain. That is a matter which is left for trial. However, as I have tried on a number of other occasions, and with regard to other evidence, I have endeavoured to resolve issues, if possible, either by motion or by consent. Those issues which I think would be very time consuming on a trial -- of trial time. With that said, we had taken the linkage chart and I again say that it is, in my mind, superficial because it mixes something which is forensic and something which is a fact yet to be established at trial. Dr. Djunic cannot pass upon testimony of a witness who has not yet testified, whom he does not know and cannot pass upon that within the scope of his review, and again I stress that this was only a review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What has he done for his 11.000 dollars which I understand he's been authorised?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I will let Mr. Kostich speak to that. He has been in contact, has met, as well as I have, at lengthy conferences, pointing out problems with the exhumation reports, but he has -- Mr. Kostich has reviewed the linking chart with Dr. Djunic and he can report to you the outcome of that consultation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTICH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Use the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTICH
utterances.text: Your Honour. My consultations with Mr. Djunic were many-fold. One of the things that he had to do is to spend an inordinate amount of time in reviewing, literally, I would say, thousands and thousands of pages. I have not counted them, Judge, but they are three feet or four feet worth of materials. He's gone through all of that. He has gone through a number of other matters concerning some other reports. I also reviewed the linkage chart with him. I can tell you -- the linkage chart has about 19 items on it. As far as the item number 1, which deals with the Brcko exhumations, he felt that there was a shortcoming, having to do with certain parts of that report and there were I think 60 or 70 sketches of bodies and so on, and what he requested were individual autopsy reports in order to give us a full opinion. He could not obtain those, either they are not available or for whatever reason we could not supply them with those. So one part of his opinion could not be given. He was dissatisfied as to that. Items 2 through 19 were done by other authorities in the Federation. They were court individuals, investigators, investigative judges. Those were in B/C/S. Those were of extremely great length. He had spent with me sometime discussing those. I can tell you, and I want to be fairly moderate in what I tell you, that he was completely dissatisfied with the work that was done during those exhumations, in terms of every aspect of the work, both in terms of the autopsies -- well first of all the exhumations, number 1. The anthropological, as well as the autopsies. He was dissatisfied with the identification procedures. He made some comments about standards that would be applied in those situations. He was very unhappy about those standards. And for that reason, his advice to the Defence team was that he really could not accept the findings in those reports, either in regard to the cause of death, the time of death, and the identification of the bodies. And that was rendered to us during the consultations. So on all these issues, judge, our expert is dissatisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say dissatisfied, has he put pen to paper at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTICH
utterances.text: I don't know, judge, because Mr. Brashich handled that part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm sure that he's literate and can put pen to paper. However it was my specific instruction that I did not wish to get a written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I don't know if nothing is in writing how you're going to go on with this. How you're going to cross-examine. You better get him to put something in writing otherwise you're not going to be able to cross-examine these witnesses. Also he has this sum of money and there ought to be something in writing to show for it. That will be a matter for the Registry to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've taken your comments under advisement but, again, I want to make it very clear that we have fully complied with the provisions of the expert witness Rule. To go on and move on to another matter, Your Honour, I would seek a clarification. Perhaps I misheard. Is this Chamber, which is not going to hear this case, admitting en masse the 2.000 some core documents? Is that the ruling of this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Subject to objection, which you take during the time when they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Either they are admitted or they are not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are admitted to -- subject to -- you can object if you want when they come to be called in the usual way. What we are trying to do is to reduce the number which should be available for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could it possibly, so the record is clear, be a better approach, Your Honour, that the Prosecution be limited to 2.000 core documents and then those 2.000 core documents will be dealt with by the Trial Chamber that will try this case and then I will have an opportunity of -- to object? At least this is the practise in the jurisdiction from which I come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean whichever way we word it, you will have the opportunity to object. There is no question of that. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 355 to 358.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A clarification, Your Honour, with the Court's ruling that it will make rulings and issue orders which would be then subject to, if you want to call it that, review by the actual trying Trial Chamber, with regard to requests for certification for appeal, could I make an oral motion that the right to make a certification for appeal for your -- for this Trial Chamber's orders be stayed until the Trial Chamber that will try this case either adopts your ruling or amends it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what appeals have we got at the moment? Are you appealing anything at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, what I'm saying, Your Honour, if tomorrow this Trial Chamber rules on 92 bis applications, if the Defence feels aggrieved by your order, I have a specific period of time within which to seek certification. However, you have said, Your Honour has said, that this order could be either adopted or amended, amplified by the Trial Chamber. What I'm suggesting, Your Honour, by my oral application is that the time to seek certification will not commence to run until such time as the actual Trial Chamber adopts Your Honour's ruling or modifies it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If at any stage you want to appeal one of our rulings, then you can add that to the application, but it's ruling in a vacuum at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm just asking for the time within which to file certification to be extended

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, when you -- when or if you want to appeal an order that we've made, you can apply to us for an extension, if you want to, for time. But at the moment, we are not going to rule in a vacuum on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Again, a clarification, Your Honour, with regard to the 92 bis, I believe Mr. Harmon might have misspoke. That is deferred to the new Trial Chamber, am I correct, the 92 bis motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 92 bis motion will be. We shall word our order about witnesses in this way: That the Prosecution will be able, it will be for them to select their witnesses, to call a certain number of witnesses per municipality, live. They will also have leave to call a certain number, subject to Rule 92 bis, but that ruling will be subject to the decision of the Trial Chamber as to whether those witnesses are called live or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber could then rule whether they be called live -- sorry, whether they be admitted, I should say, rather than called under Rule 92 bis, whether they be admitted subject to cross-examination, live, as we did in Milosevic with a great number of witnesses, or whether they be called live. It will be a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. As you are aware, having read the Rule 65 ter conference, the issue on the video as to the death of Yugoslavia is now moot. The Defence has withdrawn that motion and has reserved its right to deal with that problem with the new Trial Chamber. The last thing which I have on my -- it's not a wish list, it's a list -- is the video clips which proves an old adage of the United States army, never volunteer. The individual who had been transcribing and could identify that, is not available at this present time. I have consulted with Ms. Featherstone, senior legal adviser, and we will try and resolve this particular matter in some fashion, Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, my co-counsel also asks me for a clarification from the Trial Chamber as to the adjudicated facts. The adjudicated facts motion again is being deferred to the new Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The position about that is, I think haven't yet seen your response. You were due to respond by the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you do that, we will consider the position. It may be that we will defer it, but we will consider the position in light of your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, the intercept motion is also going to be deferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deferred, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could I suggest, Your Honour, that that -- that's one motion that perhaps this Trial Chamber should actively undertake to decide. The Krajisnik Defence is aware that a like motion has been made in the Milosevic case and the response by the Prosecution in the Milosevic case, in one or two foot notes, refers to the legal arguments made by the Krajisnik Defence. Perhaps it would be of sound judicial economy that this Chamber decides both motions, since the arguments and the issues, at least from what I see, and of course I do not participate in the Milosevic case, are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: While the intercept question could be seen as a purely legal question which could be decided by the Pre-Trial Chamber before the trial, for my part, I think it is a matter that would be better dealt with by the Trial Chamber in the context of the evidence as a whole. So I concede, yes, it could be dealt with as a purely legal matter, but I think it would be better dealt with by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Judge Robinson, as most often happens, when I hear Your Honours speak I change my mind and I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Would that all arguments were settled so rapidly. The other matter, Mr. Brashich, which I should have raised with you is this: That the Prosecution are going to be ready in mid-February. Can we hear from you, if you anticipate you could be ready or would be ready at that time? We understand you wanted early January to be avoided. It would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We said mid-February.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I think that we can accommodate and be ready for that date, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTICH
utterances.text: Your Honour I was just still agreeing with Mr. Brashich and what he told Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's behind you. Mr. Krajisnik wants to say something. Let him say something. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Krajisnik [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say that I'm sorry that this Trial Chamber is leaving this case, won't be trying the case, although over the three years that I've spent here, I didn't have the luck that you solve some of the requests put forward by our Defence counsel and placed before you, but I had the profound conviction that I can prove my defence that I'm not guilty before this Trial Chamber, and so, as you are leaving, at the end, I should like to be allowed to say a few words here and now today. As far as I can see, the trial should begin sometime in mid-February. The Prosecution has, in an ambitious way and so has my Defence, put forward this, and as a layman, I'm not able to say in a competent manner whether everything will be trial ready by mid-February but I -- what I should like to ask you would be to make a positive ruling, a positive decision, at this final outset, and that is to enable my Defence counsel to engage a greater number of investigators and consultants which the Registrar need not pay. They can be paid from other fund so that in the short space of time that we have left, we make up for lost time previously. That is one request that I should like to make and I do ask you to accept it. My second request is the following: As the witnesses who are potential witnesses, might I say, are either in the forests or are -- have gone underground, it is difficult to come by those witnesses. There are secret indictments so people are afraid and my Defence team have their own family members. So they don't need to be paid but may they please be allowed to stay on the Defence team? Because people are very unwilling to make statements to people they don't know but they would be willing to do so to family members of my defence team. And my third request is as follows: May be allowed to have a co-counsel, just like all teams have a foreign Defence counsel, an American or somebody from the U.K., and may I have a co-counsel from Republika Srpska who would coordinate all the work to be done, who would be able to contact the authorities and I would have the right to have telephone communication with this co-counsel. I took it upon myself to write a letter and make a request. This was because of my impotence. I felt that all the other clients do have the right to do so and that there was a misunderstanding that arose. I have no criticisms to make. The only thing that I should like to ask you would be to let me have all the means available to prove in this short space of time that I am not guilty, and you will see in the trial to come that I am not guilty indeed. But never mind about that, what is important for me is to prove to the Court, to the Tribunal, that I'm not guilty and I won't be able to do this unless I'm given all the means at my disposal to go into all the details. I wish you every success in your future work and I'm sure you'll be able to deal with the cases you are dealing with most successfully. Thank you once again for allowing me to speak, to have this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider the requests made by the accused. As for the other matters, what I've said we would do is to fix a date for trial, which we do for mid-February. We can't fix a more precise date than that at the moment. Meanwhile, we shall in due course recommend the President to assign a new Trial Chamber to this case. We are not in a position to -- we've come to the conclusion -- to review or to make an order setting up any kind of time limit for the Prosecution. That will be a matter for the Trial Chamber trying the case. However, we have, as I indicated earlier, reviewed the number of witnesses who should be available to the Prosecution. We have in mind that as far as the municipalities are concerned, that there should be 89 live witnesses and 176 witnesses to be called under Rule 92 bis, all live, if the Trial Chamber so determines. As to the remaining category of witnesses, we have noted in relation to the international witnesses that of the 19 listed, four relate to the co-accused, and therefore could be excluded, and of the 15 remaining, we take the view that 13 should be called live, two under Rule 92 bis or as I said earlier, live, if the Chamber so determines. As for the 22 general witnesses or miscellaneous witnesses as they are called, we take the view that 7 should be called live and 15 under Rule 92 bis. There are, it seems, 15 experts who should be called live. And that makes a total for the Prosecution of 124 live witnesses, 193 under Rule 92 bis or live if the Trial Chamber so determines. The Prosecution to make its own selection, of course. And as the Rules provide, the order may be varied on application to the Trial Chamber. Mr. Harmon, we didn't hear you on the subject of the exhibits. The suggestion was that of your 11.217, we reduce them to 2.000 or so, however many the core documents are and you would have to apply for leave to call any more. Would you care to address us on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are satisfied with that ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will make the ruling in those terms. I should say that this order which I've given today will be put into written form and the written form will be, of course, the applicable order, rather than what I've said today. Unless there are any other matters which anyone wishes to address us on -- the Senior Legal Officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's been a long two days and my mind is fuzzy. Regardless of the wording, is it the ruling of the Court that the 2.000 -- the Prosecution will be limited to the 2.000-some-odd core documents and then only by leave of the new Trial Chamber can additional documents come in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That will be the ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 3.19 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Trial Chamber and senior legal officer confer]
